# 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado

## Overview

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was a large, long-tracked, destructive EF3 tornado that occurred during the afternoon and early evening of April 27, 2011, as part of a major tornado outbreak affecting the eastern half of the United States from April 25 to 28, 2011. 

According to a post-event survey by the National Weather Service (NWS) office in Birmingham, Alabama, the tornado was rated EF-3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with estimated maximum winds of about 145 mph (233 km/h), a total path length of approximately 72.13 miles (116.1 km), and a maximum width of about 1,760 yards (1.0 mile). It resulted in 7 fatalities and 50 injuries as it moved across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties in central Alabama. 

The tornado affected multiple rural communities and small towns along its track, including areas near Tishabee and Forkland in Greene County, Sawyerville and nearby communities in Hale County, and the community of Eoline and surrounding areas in Bibb County. 

Within the broader context of the April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was one of numerous significant tornadoes that occurred on April 27, 2011, a day on which about 207 tornadoes were confirmed nationwide and four reached EF5 intensity, contributing to what has been described by the National Weather Service as one of the largest, deadliest, and most destructive tornado outbreaks in United States history. 

## Meteorological background and warning process

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado formed during a multi-day severe weather episode from April 25 to 28, 2011, during which a powerful storm system produced a widespread tornado outbreak across the eastern half of the United States. 

Across central Alabama, the NWS Birmingham office documented an extensive outbreak of tornadoes on April 27, 2011, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, as part of this larger synoptic-scale event. 

Based on the Birmingham storm survey, the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado developed in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River, just west of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive, around 5:30 p.m. Central Daylight Time, and tracked generally northeastward for over an hour before dissipating just northeast of Marvel in Bibb County by about 6:55 p.m. CDT. 

The NWS Birmingham report states that tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties from approximately 4:50 p.m. until 7:45 p.m. CDT, covering the period during which the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was on the ground. 

## Tornado path and intensity

According to the NWS Birmingham storm survey, the tornado initially produced EF1 damage after touching down near the Tombigbee River in far southwest Greene County and moving northeast across rural portions of Greene County north of Forkland, before intensifying to EF2 intensity while still in Greene County. 

The tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and entered Hale County west of Sawyerville, then crossed Alabama Route 14 just north of Sawyerville, where surveyors concluded that it intensified to EF3 strength with estimated winds of 145 mph. 

Continuing northeast, the tornado moved across County Road 18, County Road 21, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram in Hale County, maintaining EF3 strength and producing extensive structural damage in these areas. 

The storm survey indicates that the tornado then entered the Talladega National Forest near Ingram and tracked northeastward toward the Bibb County line, where it caused significant tree damage along its path within the national forest. 

Upon entering Bibb County, the tornado moved through the community of Eoline, where the NWS survey rated the damage as EF3 with estimated winds of 145 mph, before the tornado weakened to EF2 intensity as it crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton and finally dissipated just northeast of Marvel. 

## Impacts

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado caused 7 fatalities and 50 injuries along its 72.13-mile path through Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, according to the NWS Birmingham survey. 

In Hale County, particularly in and near the community of Sawyerville, the tornado produced extensive structural damage as it crossed Alabama Route 14 and nearby roads, destroying numerous mobile homes and single-family residences as well as at least one church, and downing thousands of trees. The survey attributes roughly 40 injuries and 6 of the 7 total fatalities to this portion of the track. 

Within the Talladega National Forest, the tornado caused widespread tree damage, with the NWS survey describing significant tree loss along its path in the forested areas of Hale and Bibb counties. 

In Bibb County, the tornado inflicted severe damage in the Eoline area, where numerous mobile homes and single-family houses sustained minor to major damage and about a dozen such structures were destroyed. The tornado also demolished the Eoline Fire Department building and another business. One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire department, and at least 10 additional injuries were reported in this segment of the path. 

After leaving Eoline and crossing Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, the tornado, then rated EF2 with estimated winds of about 125 mph, continued to damage or destroy several mobile homes and single-family residences near County Road 26 before weakening and lifting near Marvel; along the later portions of the path, thousands of additional trees were reported downed. 

## Context within the April 27, 2011 outbreak

The NWS Mobile/Pensacola office notes that the April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak produced a total of 343 tornadoes across the United States, including approximately 207 tornadoes on April 27 alone, and that four of the April 27 tornadoes reached EF5 intensity, underscoring the scale and severity of the event in which the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado occurred. 

Within Alabama, the outbreak affected multiple National Weather Service County Warning Areas, with the NWS Mobile/Pensacola office documenting that only one of the 207 April 27 tornadoes occurred in its jurisdiction—an EF3 tornado in Choctaw County whose track spanned three different warning areas—while numerous other tornadoes, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, were documented by the NWS Birmingham office in central Alabama.

**_Sawyerville-Eoline (Greene,Hale and Bibb Counties)EF-3 Tornado April 27, 2011_** **Rating: [(_Click for EF Scale_)](https://www.weather.gov/bmx/enhancedfujitascale)****EF-3** **Estimated Maximum Wind:****145 mph** **Injuries/Fatalities:******50 Injuries /7 Fatalities**** **Damage Path Length:****72.13 miles** **Maximum Path Width:****1760 yards (1 mile)** **Approximate Start Point/Time:********32.6152/-88.0543 at 530 pm****** **Approximate End Point/Time:**************33.1524/-86.9898 at 655 pm************ **National Weather Service meteorologists surveyed multiple tracks across Greene, Hale and Bibb Counties. It has been determined that the damage was consistent with a strong tornado. The tornado touched down in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River just West of Tishabee on County Road 69 near Head Drive, and headed northeast across rural Greene County north of Forkland. At least 4 mobile homes, 3 outbuildings, and 2 churches were damaged or destroyed along with numerous trees. Two minor injuries were noted in Greene County. The track started as an EF-1 but increased to an EF-2 rating while in Greene County.** **The tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and into Hale County west of Sawyerville. The tornado crossed AL Route 14, just north of Sawyerville, where it intensifyed to an EF-3 rating with winds of 145 mph. As the tornado continued northeast, it crossed CR 18, CR 21, AL Hwy 69 south of Harper Hill, and CR 29 east of Ingram. Extensive structural damage was noted in the these locations, which resulted in at least 40 injuries and 6 fatalities. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes and one church were damaged or destroyed. Thousands of trees were knocked down. The tornado moved into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, where it caused significant tree damage to the Bibb County line.** **The tornado tracked northeastward where it caused significant tree damage in the national forest. The tornado moved through Eoline and caused significant structural damage consistent with an EF-3 rating and winds of 145 mph. Numerous mobile homes and single family homes sustained minor to major damage. A dozen mobile homes and single family homes were destroyed. In addition, the Eoline Fire Dept and another business were destroyed. One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire dept. At least 10 other injuries were noted. The tornado continued northeast and crossed AL Hwy 5, south of West Blocton where it weakened slightly to an EF-2 with winds of 125 mph. Several mobile homes and single family homes sustained major damage or were destroyed near CR 26. Along the path, thousands of trees were downed. **April 27th, 2011

 Tornado Outbreak Across The Deep South**

[![Image 4](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/2011_April27.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/2011_April27.png)

The 27 April 2011 Tornado Outbreak across the Deep South was part of another 3-day tornado outbreak (April 25-28), which was one of the largest, deadliest, and most destructive tornado outbreaks in US history. In total, there were 343 tornadoes over this 3-day period with 207 tornadoes on April 27 alone. **4 of the 207 tornadoes on April 27th were EF-5.** There was only 1 tornado (out of the 207) that occurred across the NWS Mobile/Pensacola County Warning Area (CWA) on April 27th - an EF-3 that crossed into northwestern Choctaw County, AL. To view the staggering amount of tornado reports from the Deep South submitted to the Storm Prediction Center (SPC), head over to the [SPC Severe Weather Archive](http://www.spc.noaa.gov/exper/archive/event.php?date=20110427).

[![Image 5](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/SPC_reports.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/SPC_reports.png)

Although the majority of the NWS Mobile CWA was spared during this historic tornado outbreak, northern Choctaw County, AL certainly was not. A regional view of supercell rotation tracks (courtesy of the National Severe Storms Laboratory) on April 27th shows the extent of the outbreak and just how far south it extended (clipping the northern portion of our CWA).

[![Image 6](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/Fig1.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/Fig1.jpg)

**Northern Choctaw County, AL EF-3 Tornado**

[![Image 7](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/2011April27_TorTrack.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/mob/events/2011_April27_Tornado/2011April27_TorTrack.jpg) At approximately 710pm, a strong tornado moved from extreme northeastern Clarke County, MS (NWS Jackson CWA) into northern Choctaw County approximately 4 miles southwest of the town of Yantley. This tornado remained on the ground for the entire width of northern Choctaw County. The tornado crossed the Tombigbee River near the town of Oakchia in Choctaw County and then continued into NWS Birmingham's CWA at approximately 747pm.

This tornado traveled nearly parallel to County Road 32 producing EF-2 damage with sporadic EF-3 damage along its path. There was considerable tree damage along the entire path with many trees snapped off above ground level and some trees completely uprooted. Extensive house and structure damage was noted along the path with EF-3 damage to one house where the roof was tossed, thus causing the exterior walls to collapse. Several mobile homes along the path were completely destroyed.

The image to the right shows the supercell rotation track (times noted alongside the pins),the surveyed damage locations (colored triangles), and select screenshots of the supercell’s reflectivity and velocity between 710pm and 747pm. [Note: Choctaw County, AL is far from all radar sites in the region, so the radar base reflectivity and velocity at the lowest cut are still around 10,000 feet above ground level.] The tornado’s track appears to be continuous along a 23.7 mile track with maximum winds of 150mph across the northern portion of Choctaw County, AL. [Note: this tornado spanned 3 different NWS CWA's - Jackson, Mobile, and Birmingham - so the total path length was much larger than denoted above.]
